name: The T Street Champion Linden

location.address: 3819 T St NW, Washington, DC (street tree, public sidewalk)

story:
The city's own arborists have written four words into this linden's record that no other linden in their care carries, "City Tree champion of its genus." It stands in a tree box on the sidewalk outside 3819 T Street NW, on a residential block in Burleith, and by the judgement of the people who prune it, it is the best basswood Washington looks after.

The numbers behind the note are plain. The trunk measures about 141 centimetres across at chest height, which works out to roughly 4.4 metres round. Laser survey fields in the same record suggest a crown about 22 metres high, spreading over something like 375 square metres. When an arborist checked it on 7 October 2026, its condition went down as Excellent.

That is all the paperwork says, and it is worth being clear about what it is. The champion label is the inventory's own wording, an arborist's note rather than the result of a published contest, and the city's record is the only source for this tree. It carries no planting date either. Nobody has dated this linden. If you know when the trees on this stretch of T Street went in, or have an old photograph of the block, tell us.

American basswood is a tree of eastern woodland. Finding the city's best one growing out of a square of pavement is half the pleasure of the walk.

name: The Hardy Park Elm

location.address: Hardy Park (DC Parks and Recreation), Foxhall / Palisades side of Georgetown, Washington, DC

story:
Every so often a city crew comes to Hardy Park and injects this elm, and the record of it sits in Washington's tree inventory beside the measurements. The injection is the standard defence against Dutch elm disease, the fungus that has taken most of the great American elms that once lined the streets of the eastern United States. This one is still standing, and still being looked after, pruned in 2025, inspected again in May 2026 and rated Good.

It is worth the trouble. The trunk is about 163 centimetres across at chest height, which puts its girth at roughly 5.1 metres, and it is one of the two largest American elms in the city's inventory of public street and park trees. The other is about two kilometres north on 38th Street in Glover Park. What sets this one apart is room. The record gives its crown an area of about 615 square metres, the spread of an elm that grew in the open with nothing to lean away from.

Everything else in Hardy Park is small. Within twenty metres the inventory finds only two young Kwanzan cherries and a redbud, which makes the elm look even bigger than it is.

The city's record is the only source for this tree, and it gives no planting date. Nobody has put an age on it. If you know the history of Hardy Park, or remember the elm when it was younger, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its crown, a wide open-grown American elm about 5.1 metres round. It stands in Hardy Park, towering over the park's small cherries and redbud.

name: The 38th Street Elm

location.address: 2716 38th St NW, Washington, DC (street tree, public sidewalk)

story:
Two American elms in northwest Washington have trunks within a centimetre and a half of each other, and they could hardly have grown up more differently. One spreads across open lawn in Hardy Park. This one grew on a sidewalk in Glover Park, outside 2716 38th Street NW, with houses on one side and traffic on the other.

The city's tree inventory measures it at about 162 centimetres across at chest height, roughly 5.1 metres round, which places it among the three or four largest American elms on the city's books. The street shows in the crown. Laser survey fields in the record give it a height of about 24 metres but a spread of only around 240 square metres, well under half the area of the Hardy Park elm. The elm went up rather than out.

It survives because it is looked after. The record notes a pruning in March 2026 and an injection, the treatment that protects American elms against Dutch elm disease, and an inspection in May 2026 rated it Good. The nearest street tree of any size is a scarlet oak of about 61 centimetres across, less than half its width.

The inventory is the only source, and it does not say when the tree was planted. Its age is unknown. If you know the story of this block, or when the elms of Glover Park went in, tell us.

name: The Constitution Avenue Elm

location.address: 2200 block of Constitution Ave NW, Washington, DC (street tree beside the Mall at 23rd Street)
location.neighbourhood: Foggy Bottom / West Potomac Park edge

story:
A stand of big old trees on private ground at 2101 Constitution Avenue, several of them thicker than this one, went into the city's records as removed in October 2026. This elm, on the public pavement at the western end of the Mall, is the one still standing in that corner of Foggy Bottom.

It is the largest of a row of American elms along the north side of Constitution Avenue near 23rd Street. The city's tree inventory gives it a trunk about 144 centimetres across at chest height, roughly 4.5 metres round. Its neighbours are clearly smaller. One elm about 60 metres away measures some 109 centimetres across, another within 20 metres about 62. Laser survey fields in the same record put the crown at around 26 metres high.

The tree has been through work. The record notes a heavy prune in December 2023, and at its last inspection, in May 2025, the arborist rated it Good.

It also fits a short walk. The Willow Oak Circle in Constitution Gardens is about 320 metres east, and the cork trees of the FDR Memorial are about a kilometre south.

The city's inventory is the only source, and it gives no planting date. Nobody has dated this elm. If you know when this stretch of Constitution Avenue was planted, tell us.

name: The East Capitol Street Elm

location.address: 322 East Capitol St NE, Washington, DC (street tree on East Capitol Street)

story:
Official records rarely have a sense of humour, but the arborist who inspected this elm in May 2026 summed it up in the city's tree inventory as "A real thiccums!" The trunk earns it. On East Capitol Street, a few blocks east of the Capitol, it measures about 137 centimetres across at chest height, roughly 4.3 metres round.

The same note carries the less cheerful news. The elm has been dying back since 2019, a broken hanging limb was taken down in May 2026, and the inspector rated its condition Fair rather than Good. It is a big old tree in decline, and the record says so plainly. Laser survey fields in the inventory give the crown a height of about 16 metres, modest for a trunk of this width.

Its neighbours make the size easy to read. Within twenty metres stand two Princeton elms, a cultivar of American elm bred to resist Dutch elm disease, about 13 and 51 centimetres across, and a smaller American elm of about 48. None of them comes close.

Capitol South Metro is about 800 metres away, and the Olmsted tuliptree on the Capitol grounds is roughly 600 metres west, so this elm fits easily into a walk around Capitol Hill. Garfield Park's big zelkova is about a kilometre south.

The inventory is the only source for this elm, and it records no planting date. Nobody has dated it. If you know when East Capitol Street's elms went in, tell us.

name: The Volta Park Osage Orange

location.address: Volta Park, 1500 block of 34th St NW, Georgetown, Washington, DC

story:
No Osage orange in Washington's tree inventory comes anywhere near this one. In Volta Park, on 34th Street in Georgetown, it measures about 145 centimetres across at chest height, roughly 4.6 metres round. The other Osage oranges growing around it, and there are several, run from about 50 to 97 centimetres.

That is a big trunk for the species. Osage orange is a tough, thorny tree from the south-central United States, better known for its heavy green fruit and rot-proof wood than for its size, and few grow this broad. So the figure deserves a caveat. It is an arborist's measurement in the city's own records, and those records do not say whether the trunk is a single stem or several grown together. Until somebody checks, read it as a measurement of what stands there, not a claim about a single trunk.

The tree has had its knocks. It lost a branch about ten centimetres thick in the January 2025 snowstorm, and at its last inspection, in August 2026, it was rated Fair. Laser survey fields in the record give the crown a height of about 19 metres.

Volta Park is a short walk from Montrose Park and Dumbarton Oaks Park, which makes this an easy addition to a Georgetown tree walk. The city's inventory is the only source, and it gives no planting date. Nobody knows how old these Osage oranges are, or why a group of them grows here. If you do, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the largest of the group of Osage oranges in Volta Park, its trunk about 4.6 metres round and far heavier than the others beside it. It stands in Volta Park, Georgetown.

name: The Banks Place Willow Oak

location.address: Park opposite 6112 Banks Pl NE (6201 Banks Pl NE in the inventory), Washington, DC

story:
Every other tree in this small Ward 7 park is a sapling, and the one that is not is the largest willow oak in the city's inventory of park trees. It stands across the road from 6112 Banks Place NE, in far northeast Washington, near the Maryland line.

The city's arborists measure its trunk at about 171 centimetres across at chest height, roughly 5.4 metres round. Laser survey fields in the record give it a crown about 27 metres tall spreading over some 527 square metres, a crown that has had the open ground to itself. Around it, the inventory lists young honeylocusts, horse chestnuts and a hackberry, all of them a few centimetres thick. A second, smaller willow oak, about 136 centimetres across, grows some 200 metres east along the same street.

It is not the biggest willow oak in Washington. The one in the National Arboretum, on federal ground the city's inventory does not cover, is larger again. But no willow oak the city lists on its own park ground comes close. At its last inspection, in July 2025, it was rated Good, with deadwood pruned out.

Willow oaks grow fast, which is why a trunk this wide need not be very old. The city's record gives no planting date, and nobody has dated the tree. If you know the history of this park, tell us.

name: The Lansburgh Park Elm

location.address: Lansburgh Park, 1098 Delaware Ave SW, Washington, DC

story:
The arborist's verdict on this elm, written straight into Washington's tree inventory, fits on one line, "Awesome tree; Leaning over dog park." Both halves hold up. In Lansburgh Park in Southwest, the American elm leans out over the park's dog park, and its trunk measures about 130 centimetres across at chest height, roughly 4.1 metres round.

It has taken some punishment. In the wind storm of 30 April 2021 it lost a limb about 20 centimetres thick, and laser survey fields in the record give it a crown only about 12 metres high, modest for a trunk this wide. Even so, at its last inspection, in May 2026, the city rated it Good.

It has the park to itself. The only other tree within twenty metres, according to the inventory, is a pawpaw a few centimetres thick, so there is no mistaking which trunk the note is about.

Waterfront Metro is about 500 metres away, roughly a seven-minute walk, and the Caucasian elm at the Botanic Garden is about 1.2 kilometres north, so the tree can end a walk south from the Mall.

The city's inventory is the only source, and it does not say when the elm was planted. Nobody has dated it. If you know, tell us.

name: The Garfield Park Zelkova

location.address: Garfield Park, Capitol Hill (aligned with 146 F St SE), Washington, DC

story:
"Looking pretty good!" is not the language anyone expects from a government database, but it is what the city arborist wrote about this zelkova in September 2025. It is also an understatement. In Garfield Park, a few minutes' walk south of the Capitol, this is the largest Japanese zelkova in Washington's inventory of street and park trees.

The trunk measures about 130 centimetres across at chest height, roughly 4.1 metres round. Two other zelkovas stand within twenty metres of it, and they are about 40 and 47 centimetres across, so the old tree has well over twice their width. Laser survey fields in the record give it a crown about 19 metres tall, covering some 340 square metres of the park.

Zelkova is an East Asian relative of the elm, with the same vase of upswept branches, and in Japan the oldest ones are temple trees many centuries old. This one makes no such claim. The city's record gives no planting date, and nobody has dated it. If you know when Garfield Park's zelkovas were planted, tell us.

Capitol South Metro is about 500 metres away. The big elm on East Capitol Street and the Olmsted tuliptree on the Capitol grounds make this an easy three-tree loop around Capitol Hill.

name: The Harvard Street Willow Oak

location.address: 1661 Harvard St NW, Washington, DC (street tree, public sidewalk)

On Harvard Street, between Columbia Heights and Mount Pleasant, one willow oak has grown to nearly twice the width of every oak around it. It stands on the sidewalk in front of 1661 Harvard Street NW, and the city's tree inventory measures its trunk at about 156 centimetres across at chest height, roughly 4.9 metres round.

The comparison is right there on the block. Within twenty metres, the inventory lists two pin oaks of about 79 and 86 centimetres and another willow oak of about 83. Same street, similar trees, and this one is in a different league. Laser survey fields in the record give it a crown about 27 metres tall spreading over some 470 square metres, enough to shade a good stretch of the street.

It is also in good health. At its last inspection, in June 2025, the arborist rated it Excellent, noting only deadwood to take out.

Columbia Heights Metro is about 700 metres away, roughly a nine-minute walk. The inventory is the only source for this tree, and it records no planting date. Nobody has dated this willow oak. If you know when Harvard Street was planted, tell us.

name: Alexandria Bicentennial Sweet Gum

location.address: Alexandria National Cemetery, 1450 Wilkes Street, Alexandria, VA 22314
location.neighbourhood: Old Town Alexandria (Virginia), about 30 minutes from downtown DC by Metro (Blue/Yellow Line to King St-Old Town, then about a 10 minute walk)

location_site.name: Alexandria National Cemetery, below the flagpole

story:
In the 1970s, as the United States prepared for its two-hundredth birthday, the City of Alexandria went looking for trees old enough to have stood through the Revolution. It found seventeen, gave each a plaque, and called them Living Witnesses of the American Revolution. By the city's own count, only two of the originals still stand on public land. This sweet gum, below the flagpole in Alexandria National Cemetery, is one of them. The other is a willow oak on the Holmes Run Trail.

The witnesses have been dropping out for decades. A local newspaper counted six of the seventeen still standing in 2004. Today the city names just two on public land.

What the paperwork does not give is a number. No source we have seen publishes this sweet gum's girth or height, and the city's page puts no age on it. The Revolutionary title says the people who chose it believed it was alive in the 1770s, but that belief comes without a measurement behind it, so treat it as the designation it is rather than a dated fact. If you have measured the tree or know its history, tell us.

The cemetery is open daily from sunrise to sunset, and King St-Old Town Metro is about ten minutes away on foot. Visit quietly. It is a national cemetery, and the tree stands among the graves.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the sweet gum at the foot of the flagpole in Alexandria National Cemetery, the tree the city names as standing below the flag. It stands off Wilkes Street.

name: The Alexandria Bicentennial Willow Oak
age_estimate: about 320 years, by the City of Alexandria's estimate (likely around 1707)

location.address: Holmes Run Trail, opposite Beatley Central Library, about 100 yards in from the Duke Street entrance, Alexandria, VA

story:
By the City of Alexandria's reckoning, this willow oak was probably a seedling around 1707, a quarter of a century before George Washington was born. When the city surveyed it in 1976 the estimate was 270 years, and the arithmetic has held since. In 1977 it was designated Alexandria's Bicentennial Tree.

It is also enormous. Measured in November 2024, the trunk is 208 inches round, about 5.3 metres, and the tree stands 116 feet tall, about 35 metres, with a crown 105 feet across. The city scored it at 350 points, the formula American big-tree registers use to add girth, height and spread together. It has not come through untouched. A large limb has gone from one side.

It is one of seventeen trees Alexandria named in the 1970s as Living Witnesses of the American Revolution, and by the city's count one of only two still standing on public land. The other is a sweet gum in Alexandria National Cemetery in Old Town.

The age is an estimate, not a ring count, and the city does not publish how it was made. On our Washington map the white oak at Travilah in Maryland is still reckoned older.

Getting here takes commitment. The tree stands about 100 yards in from the Duke Street entrance to the Holmes Run Trail, opposite the Beatley Central Library, and from downtown Washington that is Metro to King St-Old Town and a bus west along Duke Street, about 45 to 50 minutes in all.

name: Japanese Chestnut at Saint John the Apostle

location.address: Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church grounds, 101 Oakcrest Manor Dr NE, Leesburg, VA 20176

location_site.name: Saint John the Apostle church grounds and cemetery, Church Street NE

story:
For a while nobody could agree what this tree was. Nominated to Virginia Tech's big-tree database in 2015, it was first listed as a European chestnut. The American Chestnut Foundation took a closer look and concluded it was a Japanese chestnut, partly because it is very old and shows no sign of chestnut blight, the disease that wiped out the American chestnut and that Asian chestnuts largely shrug off.

It grows on the grounds of Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church in Leesburg, just north of a spring house at a sharp turn of Church Street. In 2015 its trunk was 161 inches round. When the Loudoun County forester remeasured it in 2025 it had reached 171 inches, about 4.3 metres, with a height of 54 feet (16.5 metres) and a crown 55 feet across. That is a tree as wide as it is tall.

Whether it is a state champion depends on whom you ask. The county's 2025 list marks it as Virginia's champion Japanese chestnut. The Virginia Tech record says it is not. The two sources disagree, and neither explains why.

It has company. A shellbark hickory stands about seven metres away, and two more county-registered trees, a silver linden and an Atlantic white cedar, are within a hundred metres on the same grounds. No source dates any of them. If you know when the chestnut was planted, or who brought it to Leesburg, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the low, wide crown of a chestnut 4.3 metres round, beside a much taller shellbark hickory seven metres away. It stands just north of the spring house at the sharp turn of Church Street.

name: Atlantic White Cedar at Saint John the Apostle

story:
Virginia's champion Atlantic white cedar does not grow in a swamp. It grows on a church lawn in Leesburg, far inland from the coastal wetlands where its species belongs.

Atlantic white cedar is a tree of the Atlantic coastal plain, a narrow evergreen of bogs and swampy ground along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts. This one stands on the grounds of Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church, on Church Street NE, and the Loudoun County Big Tree Registry measured it in 2025 at 58 feet tall (17.7 metres), with a trunk 125 inches round (about 3.2 metres) and a crown only 31 feet across. That slim shape is typical of the species. Its score of 191 points puts it at the top of Virginia's list for its kind, according to the county.

How it got here is a mystery. No source we have found says who planted it or when, and nobody has dated it. A swamp cedar on a Piedmont church lawn was almost certainly planted, and the parish or the town may remember by whom. If you know, tell us.

It is one of four registered trees on these grounds, all within about a hundred metres of each other. The others are a Japanese chestnut, a shellbark hickory and a silver linden that is itself a Virginia champion. The cedar is the evergreen among them, standing about 45 metres east of the chestnut.

name: Silver Linden at Saint John the Apostle

location.address: Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church grounds, Church Street NE, Leesburg, VA 20176

location_site.name: Saint John the Apostle church grounds and cemetery, Church Street NE

story:
The widest trunk on the grounds of Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church belongs to a tree from the other side of the Atlantic. This silver linden measures 246 inches round, about 6.25 metres, and the Loudoun County Big Tree Registry's 2025 list marks it as Virginia's champion of its species.

That is a remarkable girth for any linden. Silver linden is native to south-eastern Europe and western Asia, a tree planted in American towns for its shade and its leaves, dark green above and silvery white beneath, so the crown flickers pale when the wind turns them. The county measured this one at 69 feet tall (21 metres), with a crown 61 feet across, for a total of 330 points. Of the four registered trees on these grounds, it has the widest trunk by a long way. The Japanese chestnut nearby is about 4.3 metres round.

Nobody seems to have written down when it went in. The county gives no age and no planting date, and no other source we know of does. A linden this broad in a churchyard is the kind of tree a parish photograph or a town history might show as a sapling. If you have one, or know the story, tell us.

The tree stands towards the north of the church grounds off Church Street NE, a few minutes' walk from King Street in the middle of town. Check for services or funerals before walking in.

name: Shellbark Hickory at Saint John the Apostle

story:
Seven metres apart on the grounds of Saint John the Apostle Catholic Church stand two trees that could hardly be built more differently. One is a Japanese chestnut, short and broad. The other is this shellbark hickory, and at 98 feet (29.9 metres) it is almost twice as tall, the tallest of the four county-registered trees on the site.

Together with the chestnut it makes one stop, and you can stand between the two and see both. The silver linden and the Atlantic white cedar complete the set within about a hundred metres.

name: Tulip Poplar at Morven Park

location.address: Morven Park, 17195 Southern Planter Lane, Leesburg, VA 20176 (near the Westmoreland Davis mansion)

story:
Ninety-seven feet is about the height of a nine-storey building, and that is how tall the Loudoun County Big Tree Registry measured this tulip tree near the mansion at Morven Park in 2025. In metres, 29.6. Its trunk is 154 inches round, about 3.9 metres, and its crown spreads 68 feet, for a total of 268 points.

Morven Park is a thousand-acre estate on the north-western edge of Leesburg, once the home of Westmoreland Davis, the Virginia governor who bought it in 1903. His wife Marguerite laid out the formal boxwood gardens in 1930. Mansion tours are ticketed, but the grounds are free to walk every day from seven in the morning until six in the evening.

What the paperwork does not tell us is how old the tree is. The Davises' arrival in 1903 and the 1930 gardens date the estate's later history, not this trunk, and no source we have seen gives a planting date or an age. A tulip tree this size could predate both, or not. Nobody knows. If you do, tell us.

The county's pin places the tree in the mansion area, but on an estate this size it is approximate, so look for a big tulip tree near the house rather than trusting the dot to the metre. Tulip trees are easy to tell apart from the rest by their square-ended leaves, shaped like the outline of a tulip.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its leaves, square-ended like a tulip's outline, on a trunk about 3.9 metres round and nearly 30 metres tall. It stands near the Westmoreland Davis mansion; the county's pin is approximate.

name: Oatlands Ginkgo
age_estimate: close to 200 years, by the estate's arborist

location.address: Oatlands Historic House and Gardens, 20850 Oatlands Plantation Lane, Leesburg, VA 20175

story:
The man who looks after Oatlands' trees calls this the third largest ginkgo in the United States. The Loudoun County Big Tree Registry's 2025 measurements make the claim easy to believe, with 103 feet in height (31.4 metres), a trunk 201 inches round (about 5.1 metres), and a crown 69 feet across, for 321 points.

It grows behind the mansion at Oatlands, a historic house and garden south of Leesburg on Route 15. Jim Donegan, the estate's tree contractor, told Middleburg Life it is close to 200 years old. That is an arborist's estimate, and no ring count or planting record has been published to back it, so it stands as his judgement rather than a date. The national ranking is his too.

The ginkgo is the only living species of a lineage older than the dinosaurs, and it shrugs off pests and pollution in a way that has made it a favourite of city streets. This one has had room and time instead. Its neighbours at Oatlands include an American boxwood canopy and yews the same article puts at around 200 years.

In November the whole crown turns butter yellow and then drops in a day or two, which is the moment to come. The gardens and grounds are open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. with a ticket. The county's 2025 measurement is the latest record of it; if you have seen it since, tell us it still stands.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fan-shaped leaves on a trunk about 5.1 metres round and over 30 metres tall. It stands behind the Oatlands mansion, inside the ticketed grounds.

It stands in Ida Lee Park, next to the Rust Farm House, a farmhouse from around 1859 at 50 Ida Lee Drive NW. If the town's figure is right, the oak was about a century old when the house went up beside it. The farmhouse now stands by the park's festival field.

name: Shumard Oak at Algonkian Regional Park

story:
Loudoun County counts this Shumard oak among the largest trees in the whole county, and it stands not in a town square but out on the trails of Algonkian Regional Park, near Sugarland Run in Sterling. The county's caption gives it as 109 feet high, 184 inches round the trunk and about 200 years old.

The 2025 registry figures put numbers on the rest. The trunk is about 4.7 metres round, the tree 33.2 metres tall, and the crown spreads 83 feet, for 313.75 points. Shumard oak is a red oak of southern bottomlands and stream banks, a big, fast tree with deeply cut, bristle-tipped leaves. The 200-year figure is the county's estimate, and it does not say how it was reached, so treat it as a forester's judgement rather than a date. If it holds, the oak was a sapling in the early 1800s.

This is the far outlier on the Leesburg page. Sterling is about 20 kilometres east of downtown, 25 to 30 minutes by car on Route 7, with no useful bus. Algonkian is a NOVA Parks park and may charge for parking at busy times, so check before you go.
